increased to 416685 in 2012-13 which is still much below the projected target of 12.5 
lakh.  The Committee feels that the shortfall in accomplishment of the target with 
respect to number of beneficiaries is mainly due to the pendi ng preparatory 
exercises, especially setting up of state and district cells and opening of bank account 
etc.  The Committee, therefore, recommends to the Ministry to make serious efforts 
with cooperation of the State Governments in putting in place the nec essary 
structures for service delivery to maximum pregnant and nursing women requiring 
cash incentives for their health, nutrition and also partial compensation for their 
wage loss. 
 
7.5 The Committee in its earlier Report had drawn attention to a scheme o f the 
Ministry Health and Family Welfare i.e Janani Suraksha Yojana which was a Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme launched in 2005 with the objective to increase institutional 
deliveries.  The Committee had recommended that a convergence of both the schemes i.e 
IGMSY and Janani Suraksha Yojana may be explored by the Ministry to avoid duplicacy 
and maximize the reach of benefits to the targeted  women.  The logic behind the 
suggestion for any kind of convergence and co -ordination was due to the fact that both 
the schemes were to be handled by AWWs and ANM functionaries of AWCs and PHCs 
respectively. 
 
7.6 The Ministry has submitted that since the objective of both the Schemes was 
different, there was no over -lapping.  Under JSY, a cash incentive was provided for 
pregnant mothers to have institutional births as well as pre and ante -natal care.  The 
Scheme primarily aimed at promoting institutional delivery.  IGMSY, on the other hand, 
provided cash incentives for improved health and nutrition to pregnant and nursing 
women for improving health and nutrition and partially compensate for wage loss.  It was 
also pointed out that there was close convergence of Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare and ICDS at the grass root level which facilitated dissemination of information 
about JSY and IGMSY schemes and availing benefits thereof.   
 
7.7 The Committee is constrained to observe that even though both the schemes, 
JSY and IGMSY cater to the needs of pregnant and nursing mothers, the Ministry 
seems reluctant to explore the possi bility of convergence of the two schemes.  The 
Committee is only making an attempt to highlight the fact that most of Indian 

women, especially those residing in rural areas are in poor state of health and are 
weak and anaemic.  Such women when pregnant nee d all kinds of support and care 
for their well -being during pregnancy and delivery and also during nursing. All 
these aspects concerning their health, nutrition and pre and ante -natal care are 
inter-connected and hence convergence of both the schemes would be desirable. The 
Committee, therefore, would like to reiterate its earlier recommendation and 
request the Ministry to explore the possibility of convergence of the two schemes for 
the well-being of pregnant mothers and avoid any over-lapping. 
 
VIII. CENTRAL ADOPTION RESOURCE AUTHORITY (CARA)

monitor and regulate in -country and inter-country adoption.  CARA primarily deals with 
adoption of orphan, abandoned and surrendered children through its 
associated/recognized adoption agencies.  It functions as a nodal body on non -
institutional child care services in the country and is envisaged as a central authority 
under the Hague Convention on Inter-country Adoption.

Information & Guidance System (CARINGS) which aimed at a transparent and friendly 
adoption process.  It offered a more child -centric approach and was an online platform 
which helped in building bridges and creating a link through a robust web -based 
management system.  Its objective was to facilitate expeditious and smooth adoption, 
ensuring transparency in the adoption process by increasing the accountability of 
implementing agencies.  The Ministry, however, submitted that much remained to be 
done as a  large number of waiting parents were there in comparison to less number of 
children available for adoption.  All adoption agencies in the country needed to update 
and upload child specific information online for expeditious adoptions.  Delays had been 
noticed at the level of Child Welfare Committees and the Court granting adoption order 
in each case.  These issues had been taken up separately with the concerned authorities.  
The Ministry further submitted that children homes all over the country needed to be 
connected with adoption agencies to enable expeditious placement of orphan, abandoned 
and surrendered children.  There was a need to stop all adoptions through unauthorized 
individuals and agencies. The waiting period of the prospective parents was beli eved to 
be minimized once more children were available in adoption in agencies. 
 
8.6 The Committee notes that as per the data provided by the Ministry till  the 
31st December, 2012, the number of in -country and inter -country adoptions had 
decreased in the year 2012-13.  The year 2011 -12 saw the total number of adoptions 
(in-country and inter-country) to 6494 whereas the total number in the year 2012-13 
(till 31.12.12) was only 3252.  It was likely to increase but the likelihood of doubling 
the numbers in the matter of three months i.e till March, 2013 seemed difficult to be 
achieved.  The Committee also notes that CARINGS was introduced to make way 
for a smooth and transparent adoption process but as admitted by the Ministry 
itself, a lot more needed to be do ne.  The Committee is of the view that the following  
steps needed to be taken for making the whole process of adoption a much more 
simpler and easier one for prospective parents:- 
 

 Children Homes to be connected directly to the adoption agencies with 
complete information about all the children in their Homes indicating the 
availability of a number of children residing in a Home 
 A maximum time frame need to be specified so that prospective parents have 
a rough idea about the possible time that would be taken  in completing all 
procedures and adopting a child.  
 Delays at the level of Child Welfare Committee and the Court granting 
adoption need to be avoided and a specified time -frame should be specified 
for these agencies too to grant adoption , thereby minimizing the endless wait 
of the prospective parents 
  Check on all adoptions through unauthorized individuals and agencies. 
 Data base of missing children should be circulated amongst all Children 
Homes from time to time to trace missing children if they had some how 
reached in any Home so as to unite them with their parents. 
 
The Committee believes that the hopes and desire of prospective parents should not 
be dashed in view of the complicated adoption procedure and their endless wait for 
adopting a child.  Moreov er, encouraging child and parent friendly procedure 
would help many orphaned, abandoned or surrendered children to find homes and 
families to blossom with warmth and love. 
 
8.7 Committee’s attention has also been drawn to the recommendation of giving 
CARA the status of a statutory structure under the JJ Act made by the Working 
Group on Child Rights for the Twelfth Plan.  The Committee is in agreement with 
the Working Group observation that such a status would result in CARA 
addressing adequately the issues r elated to monitoring, accountability, conflict of 
interest, scrutiny of agencies,data management etc. It is also high time that presence 
of CARA is in all the States. 
 
8.8 Attention of the Committee has been drawn to media reports where cases of 
exploitation of children in inter -country adoptions have been reported.  The Ministry has 
submitted that the guidelines 'Governing the Adoptions of Children 2011'  ensured 
adequate safeguards for children placed in inter -country adoption as provided in the 
Hague Convention on Protection of Children and Cooperation in respect of Inter -country 
Adoption (1993) ratified by GOI.  Each case of inter -country adoption was approved by 
competent authority of the receiving country which was obliged to provide adequate 
safeguard to the adopted children. The progress reports of the children placed in inter -

country adoption were monitored for a period of two years and the child protection 
service of the receiving country took appropriate measures in case of any abuse or 
neglect.  C hildren placed in inter -country adopted were now supported with adoption 
orders under the JJ Act to enable their citizenship expeditiously.  Moreover, amendments 
to the JJ Act were supposed to have a separate chapter on adoption.   
 
8.9 The Committee is re lieved to know that inter -country adoptions with orders 
under the JJ Act enabled the adopted children in expediting their citizenship status.  
However, there are numerous concerns regarding the inter-country adoptions, more 
so because mostly children with special need are being  placed in such adoptions.  
These children, therefore, need  much more protection from abuse and neglect and 
safeguarding of their rights.  The Committee recommends to the Ministry to 
specifically lay down guidelines and norms with res pect to inter -country adoptions 
in the JJ Acts itself as early as possible with strict monitoring provisions to check 
any abuse/neglect of the adopted child.  The Committee also notes that during 2012 -
13, CARA had undertaken inspection of 45 adoption agencies up to December, 2012. 
The Committee would appreciate if such inspections are carried out on a regular 
basis followed by corrective measures. The Committee feels that surprise 
inspections should also be made as real position at the ground level would the n 
emerge. 
 
IX. RASHTRIYA MAHILA KOSH (RMK) 
 
9.1 The Rashtriya Mahila Kosh ((RMK) is an apex micro -finance organization set up 
in 1993 for the purpose of providing micro-loans to poor women through government and 
non-government organizations, women federati ons and cooperative banks.  RMK started 
with an initial corpus of `31.00 crore which has grown to `186.00 crore.  RMK extends 
loans through a client -friendly, without collateral and hassle free mechanism for 
livelihoods, micro-enterprises, housing and fami ly needs in both rural and urban areas.  
Apart from giving micro-credit, it also builds the capacities of Self  Help Groups/women 
members and partner organizations through trainings in financial management, enterprise 
development, skills and modern practic es, as well as exposure visits and assistance in 
marketing. 

 
9.2 RMK had extended its Intermediary Micro financing Organizations (IMOs) 
network across the country including the Andaman & Nicobar Islands and the border 
areas of Jammu & Kashmir.  As on the 1 5th December, 2012, RMK had sanctioned 
cumulative loans of `340.13 crore benefitting 7,17,434 women.  Out of this, a sum of 
`229.31 crore was disbursed.  Details of loans sanctioned and released since inception 
upto 15 December, 2012 indicate considerable gaps in respect of some States as indicated

States. The Committee is surprised to note that in the case of Tamil Nadu, against a 
total amount of `74.91 crore sanctioned  since inception, funds amount ing to only 
`16.19 crore have been released upto the 15th December, 2012.  The Committee is not 

aware about the factors behind funds being duly sanctioned remaining undisbursed 
which may be for a very long time , considering the fact that RMK was set up way  
back in 1993.  Another discrepancy noticed by the Committee is the number of 
beneficiaries vis -à-vis loans disbursed.  For example , in the case of Uttarakhand, 
against `3.31 crore disbursed, there were only 2918 beneficiaries.  Likewise, while in 
Bihar, w hile `40.08 crore benefitted 16,806 women, in the case of Assam , against 
disbursement of `4.53 crore, beneficiaries were only 6605 women.  This is all the 
more revealing as loan limit per beneficiary for first loan is upto `35,000 and for 
repeat loan `50,000 taken together, the existing plus new loan.  The Committee 
strongly feels that a well -structured monitoring mechanism at all level needs to be 
put in place without any further delay.   
  
9.4 The Committee also takes note of the fact that out of `340.13 crore sanctioned 
upto the 15th December, 2012 to different States, the maximum beneficiaries have 
been the States of Andhra Pradesh ( `98.50 crore)  and Tamil Nadu ( `74.91 crore) 
having availed of half of the to tal funds sanctioned (`173.41 crore).  The Comm ittee 
strongly feels that States like U.P, Chhattisgarh, Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram need 
to be more involved.  Also , uptil now, there has been no participation from Tripura, 
Meghalaya, Goa and Chandigarh.  The Committee would appreciate if the Ministry 
takes up this issue with all the concerned States. 
  
9.5 Details of RMK -NGO Partners provided funds and loan disbursed from the 
1st January, 2012 to the 15th December, 2012 indicated that out of `25.08 crore funds 
provided, loan disbursed amounted to only `13.36 crore.  Out of 41 RMK -NGO 
Partners, there were 17 NGO Partners which although had not been provided funds 
during this period seemed to have disbursed loan, with no  details of beneficiaries 
being available.  Besides that, there were  3 NGO Partners which  neither provided 

funds nor disbursed loans but seemed to have loan beneficiaries.     This clearly 
shows that accounts of funds sanctioned, disbursed and the number of beneficiaries 
are not being maintained as per the prescribed norms.  The Committee would  
appreciate if a proper review of funds sanctioned, disbursed, recovered State wise 
and NGO –wise is undertaken and corrective measures taken accordingly. 
 
9.6 The Committee would like to point out that the modalities for  disbursal of 
loans to women benefi ciaries need to be made transparent and simple.  Apparently, 
the rate of interest at which funds are provided to IMOs and the rate of interest 
charged by IMOs from the beneficiaries are different.  The Committee is of the view 
that there should be minimum gap in the interest rate charged from NGOs and 
beneficiaries.  Also, the rate of interest charged from women beneficiaries should be 
kept at a minimal level so as to avoid  unnecessary burden of them.  The Committee 
feels that the very purpose of the Scheme  would be defeated if the interest rates 
were higher than the market rate which would certainl y discourage the poor and 
asset-less women from availing benefits under the Scheme.  Further, a time period 
needs to be specified for sanctioned but not disbursed loan amount to be returned to 
RMK by the IMOs or the NGO Partners.  This will ultimately result in funds 
reaching the beneficiaries in real need and being assisted by well -performing 
NGOs.. 
 
 
9.7 To a specific query about the status of restructuring of RM K and utilization 
of funds for RMK, the Committee has been given to understand that it was 
proposed to restructure and strengthen RMK from  the existing RMK single office 
society to Government owned Non Deposit Taking Systematically Improvement 
Non-Banking Finance Company under Section 617 of the Companies Act, with  a 
Pan India n Office network backed by need -based capital.  This was intended to 
enable RMK to respond to the growing need for micro -finance in low -income 
households on reasonable terms and condi tions and to reach out more effectively to 
poor women in the hither to less-covered or uncovered States/areas.  An EFC note 
dated the 12th August, 2011 was circulated by the Ministry to incorporate a new 
Public Limited Company, namely RMK limited by GOI by infusion of `100.00 crore 

in the first year and capitalized at `500.00 crore by the fifth year.  This was 
considered by EFC in its meeting held on the 18th June, 2012.  The EFC expressed 
concerns on whether the NBFC as proposed would be financially indepen dent as 
restructuring would add to operational costs; whether the proposed NBFC would 
access funds from the market and if so at what point and in what form; whether on 
dissolution of the Society, the funds in its accounts could be transferred to NBFC 
instead of being returned to Government account and also whether the entire 
business of the Society, including doubtful debts, decreed cases etc. could be taken 
over by NBFC.    In view of  the above, opinion of Attorney General through  the 
Ministry of Law on th e legal issue involved in the dissolution of RMK as a Society 
and transfer of its business to the proposed NBFC, was requested by this Ministry 
vide D.O. letter dated the 31st July, 2012.  The opinion/advice of the Department of 
Legal Affairs/Ld. Attorney General in the matter was awaited.  Hence, in the 
absence of approval of competent authority, expected expenditure of `100.00 crore 
(including `10.00 crore under NE) for incorporation of RMK Limited could not be 
made.  A sum of `20.00 crore (including `2.00 crore under NE) has been kept in BE 
2013-14 for incorporation of RMK Limited. 
  
9.8 The Committee takes a serious view of nil utilization of funds for RMK since 
the last three years due to the restructuring exercise of RMK which has yet not got 
the neces sary approvals.  The whole process of seeking approval for the 
restructuring exercise is moving at a snail's pace leading to no sanctioning of funds 
to States/UTs and nil performance of the scheme during the last three years.  The 
Committee can only hope t hat the restructuring exercise is expedited by the 
Ministry after seeking the necessary approvals so that women beneficiaries benefit 
from the restructured scheme with new components. 
  
X. HOSTELS FOR WORKING WOMEN 
 
10.1 The Scheme of Hostel for Working Wo men envisages provision of safe and 
affordable hostel accommodation to working, single working women, women working at 

places away from their home -town and for women being trained for employment.  Since 
its inception in 1972 -73, 902 working women hostels h ad been sanctioned under the 
Scheme all over the country, benefitting about 67,284 working women.  One new hostel 
had been sanctioned in rented premises benefitting 25 working women.   The Scheme has 
been revised with following salient features:- 
 Financial assistance for construction of hostel building to be given only on public 
land. 
 Financial assistance available for rent of the hostels run in rented premises also. 
 Provision for maintenance grant of hostel building (maximum `5.00 lakh) and 
one-time non-recurring grant for furnishings @ `7500/- per beneficiary. 
 State Government agencies, Urban Municipal Bodies, Cantonment Boards, Civil 
Society Organizations, Panchayati Raj Institutions, Self Help Groups, recognized 
College/Universities and Corporate associa tions like CII, ASSOCHAM and 
FICCI included under the revised Scheme. 
 
The State Governments had been advised to disseminate the revised guidelines of the 
Scheme and send project proposals accordingly.   
 
10.2 In the year 2012 -13, `9.00 crore was allocated  for the Scheme at the BE stage 
which was reduced to `7.47 crore at the RE stage.  Out of this, `5.75 crore had been 
released up to February, 2013 for the construction of working women's hostels across the 
country.  The Committee has been given to understa nd that due to non -receipt of 
complete and viable proposals from State Governments, only 12 projects were sanctioned 
during 2012-13 resulting in less utilization of grants/reduced RE.  State Governments had 
been advised to forward proposals after making ne ed-based demand survey for Working 
Women's Hostel.  The State Governments were reminded on the 19 th January, 2011 to 
expedite the demand surveys and send proposals as per the schematic norms of the 
revised Scheme. 
 
10.3 The Committee is of the view that th e revision of the Scheme has not helped 
in the performance of the Scheme with respect to the receipt of complete and viable 
proposals for construction of new hostels for working women.  In the year 2011, 
only one proposal was received , while 12 proposals h ad been sanctioned in the year 
2012-13.  The possibility of not getting viable and complete proposals due to revised 

norm of having public land for the construction of hostels was highlighted by the 
Committee and the Ministry had also admitted to the same and had decided to re -
consider its decision to allow construction only on public land.  However, nothing in 
this regard had been done by the Ministry in the past year 2012 -13, which has led to 
a discouraging response leading to non -receipt of viable propos als under the 
Scheme.   
 
10.4 The Committee is of the view that  the Ministry needs to assess the 
implications of the revised norms of the Scheme and take corrective measures to 
improve the performance of the Scheme with respect to construction of more host els 
for working women.  Views of the State Governments , especially the bottlenecks 
faced by them in formulation of viable proposals needed to be obtained. Result of 
need based demand surveys and feed back of the State Governments should be used 
by the Minis try to understand the practical problems faced by the States/UTs 
Further, the Committee had suggested to the Ministry to explore the possibility of 
Public-Private Partnership model in the construction of hostels for women.  The 
Committee would like to reiterate that the Ministry should explore the possibility of 
using the PPP model in the scheme for provision of many more number of hostels 
for the benefit of working women.   
 
XI. SWADHAR GREH 
 
11.1 The Scheme of Swadhar Greh is meant to reach out to those w omen who are 
victims of unfortunate circumstances and are in need of institutional support for 
rehabilitation.  The Committee observes that funds allocated for this Scheme during 
2012-13 remained under –utilised.  On a specific query in this regard, the 
Committee was informed that the new Swadhar Greh Scheme, which was 
formulated by merging the existing Swadhar and Short Stay Home Schemes, would 
be operational during the year 2012 -13.  Accordingly, an enhanced allocation of 
`90.00 crore was kept in BE 2012 -13 for release of funds to the implementing 
agencies at the improved, revised rate.  However, due to the new Scheme not getting 
all the necessary approvals, it could not be implemented as per the existing financial 
norms and allocated funds had to be reduc ed at the RE stage.  The Committee 

observes that even the reduced funds remained under -utilised.  The Committee has 
been given to understand that with an allocation of `75.00 crore for 2013 -14, all 
suitable Swadhar Homes/Short Stay Homes are envisaged to b e converted into 
Swadhar Greh and funds will be released with increased financial norms.  More 
Swadhar Greh will be set up in uncovered districts. 
 
11.2 The Committee notes that the exercise of merger of the two Schemes of Short 
Stay Homes and Swadhar Started with an evaluation study conducted by the Centre 
for Market Research and Social Development, New Delhi in 2007.  The study, 
pointing out similarities in the profile of inmates, admission procedures, 
components of the Scheme (counseling, vocational trai ning, rehabilitation) and 
follow-up procedure, recommended merger of both the schemes for better 
functioning and outcomes with lesser administrative burden.   The Committees 
would like to point out that its views and recommendation was also on the same line.  
The Committee, however, is somewhat disturbed by the undue delay taking place.  
It has taken the entire Eleventh Plan period and one year of the Twelfth Plan has 
also gone but the process of merger of two Schemes is still continuing. The 
Committee is not aware whether the suitable Short Stay Homes have been identified 
for their being brought under the revised Scheme of Swadhar.  The Committee is of 
the view that thorough review of functional Shelter Homes under both the Schemes 
covering all the aspects -infrastructure, manpower, funds available , both duly 
accounted for and unspent balances and also the problem -areas has to be made, if 
not already initiated and completed at the earliest.   This is all the more required as 
details about Short Stay Homes , allocated funds and number of beneficiaries do not 
match in the details furnished to the Committee in response to its questionnaire and 
those given in the Annual Report of the Ministry.  While as per the Annual Report 
in 2011 -12, 320 SSHs having 19,949 inmate s were released funds, as per the 
Committee Questionnaire, there were 358 SSHs having 21,417 inmates.   The 
Committee also feels that as observed by the Working Group that all the districts 
need to be covered under the Scheme so that women victims of violen ce and 
deserted/separated and destitute women have a place to go in time of need.  The 

Scheme would be better managed if State Women Commissions/State Governments 
are actively involved in the monitoring of Shelter Homes.   
 
XII. NATIONAL MISSION FOR THE EMPOWERMENT OF WOMEN 
 
12.1 The National Mission for Empowerment of Women (NMEW) was launched on 
the 8 th  March, 2010, with a view to empowering women socially, economically and 
educationally.  The Mission aims to achieve empowerment of women on all these fro nts 
by securing convergence of scheme/programmes of different Ministries/Departments of 
Government of India as well as State Governments.  Alongside, the Mission shall 
monitor and review gender budgeting by Ministries/Departments.  NMEW will facilitate 
the processes that ensure holistic empowerment of women with special focus: 
- to ensure economic empowerment of women  
- to ensure that violence against women is eliminated progressively 
- to ensure social empowerment of women with emphasis on health and 
education 
- to oversee gender mainstreaming of programmes, policies of participating 
Ministries and organizations 
- to undertake awareness generation and create, if required, structures at 
district, tehsil and village level with the involvement of Panchayats f or 
their fulfillment. 
 
NMEW has identified a three pronged strategy to achieve its objective of holistic 
empowerment of women through intervention at the policy level by reviewing 
studies/evaluations/impact assessment of programmes/schemes for gender equal ity, 
strengthening the implementation and delivery mechanism and empowering women to 
demand their entitlements.   
 
12.2 The Committee has been given to understand that during 2012 -13, the 
institutional mechanism under the mission was operationalized with t he setting up of the 
National Unit headed by the Additional Secretary and Mission Director.  It also had 
experts in the fields of poverty alleviation, social empowerment, health and nutrition, 
gender budgeting, gender rights and law enforcement, empowermen t of vulnerable and 
marginalized women, media, awareness generation, advocacy and mass communication 
and Information Technology services.  Further, the Central Monitoring Committee 
(CMC) and Inter -Ministerial Co -ordination Committee (IMCC) set up to monito r and 
facilitate convergence across Ministries met during 2012 -13.  Also, 21 States had set up 

the State Resource Centre for Women (SRCW) which operationalizes the activities of the 
Mission.  Poorna Shakti Kendras (PSKs) were to be platform/forum for women  to come 
together and explore their potential and possibilities, raise awareness about their social, 
economic and political rights and facilitate access to schemes and entitlements and build 
capabilities for promoting women's participation in decision -making.  The first such pilot 
project was launched in Pali District, Rajasthan in September, 2011 with a new model of 
delivery i.e the Convergence Model with the opening of 150 village centres.  Apart from 
all this, the Mission conducted conferences, seminars,  events and other research studies 
with the objective of achieving convergence for empowerment of women.   
 
12.3 The Committee notes that the budgetary allocation for NMEW was 22.50 crore 
for the year 2012 -13 which was reduced to `9.90 crore at the RE stag e.  The Ministry 
submitted that due to slow pace of submission of proposals on running of pilot schemes 
for achieving convergence by the States and delay in setting up of State Resource Centres 
for Women, expenditure remained low.  Hence, due to budgetary constraints of the 
Government, the RE figure was brought down in 2012 -13.  However, with the gradual 
progress in setting up of State Resource Centres for Women and progress made in 
initiating pilot schemes both by States, NGOs etc through sustained NMEW, i t was 
envisaged that the Mission could be in a position to achieve substantially increased 
expenditure in the financial year 2013-14.  Therefore, the BE 2013-14 had been increased 
to `49.50 crore. 
 
12.4 The trend of utilization of funds despite all the ini tiatives taken up under the 
Mission gives a different picture:-

The year 2010 -11 saw nil utilization of funds for the scheme .  The entire provision

The year 2011-12 witnessed under-utilization of funds and same was the case in 2012-13.  

The Committee has been given to understand that it was a newly launched scheme and its

12.5 The Committee is of the considered view that the objective of the National 
Mission for Empowerment of Women is of vital importance as it ai ms for social, 
economic an d educational empowerment of wo men by securing convergence of 
schemes/programmes of different Ministries/Departments as well as State 
Governments.  The Committee in its earlier Report had emphasized on convergence 
of schemes between different Ministries/De partments for effective implementation 
of schemes by forging a synergy between all agencies involved in the implementation 
process.  Further, NMEW was also to be involved in reviewing and monitoring 
gender-budgeting which would certainly help in holistic e mpowerment of women 
and gender mainstreaming of programmes.  The Committee believes that three 
years had passed since the Scheme had been launched but it has  yet not taken off 
properly as is evident from the under -utilization of funds and non -receipt of 
proposals for the Scheme.  Moreover, the task of setting up of State Resource 
Centres for Women in States is also  not complete.   The Committee feels that it i s 
high time that the objectives of the Mission are achieved through its proper 
implementation by ini tiating pilot convergence models and by completing the 
process of putting all the necessary structures in place and receipt of viable 
proposals from the States.  The Committee  hopes that the increased allocation of 
`49.50 crore for the year 2013 -14 is util ized fully for the implementation of the 
scheme. 
 
XIII. NATIONAL COMMISSION FOR WOMEN (NCW) 
 
13.1 The National Commission for Women (NCW) was set up in 1992 as a statutory 
apex national level body under the National Commission for Women Act, 1990.  NCW 
reviews the provisions relating to the safeguards for women under the Constitution as 
well as in other laws.  It takes up petitions from women for redressal of their grievances, 
and does promotional research for the advancement of women.   
 
 The functions/activities of the Commission include:- 
 

- to investigate and examine all matters relating to the safeguards provided for 
women under the Constitution and other laws; 
- to call for special studies or investigations into specific problems of situations 
arising out of discrimination and atrocities against women; 
- undertake promotional and educational research so as to suggest ways of 
ensuring due representation of women in all spheres and identify factors 
responsible for impending their advancement; 
- participate and ad vise on the planning process of socio -economic 
development of women; 
- evaluate the progress of the development of women under the Union and the 
States; and 
- inspect or cause to inspect a jail, remand home, women's institution or other 
place of custody where women are kept as prisoners or otherwise and take up 
with the concerned authorities for remedial action, if found necessary.

follows:-

The Committee finds the performance of NCW much better in 2011 -12 than in 2012 -13

though the Committee has been given to understand that 16637 complaints cases in 2011-
12 and 12730 (upto 31 December, 2012) were received by NCW, no information about 
the number of complaints/cases disposed off has been given. 
 
13.3 The Committee believes that the mandate of NCW is quite wide as it is a 
statutory body constituted to investigate and examine all matters relating to the 
safegtuards provided for women under the Constitution and other laws.  NCW ca n 
look into complaints and take  suo moto notice of matters relating to deprivation of 
women's rights.  Having mentioned this, the Committee would like to refer to the 
rising crimes against women in the recent times w hich violate the right to life and 

right to various freedoms enjoyed by  women citizens of the country.  Women have 
been at the receiving end most of the time , be it gender based violence and 
discrimination, sexual assault and ra pe, dowry deaths, crime and killings in the 
name of honour, trafficking, patriarchal bias in matters of family  and inheritance 
laws etc. The gruesome rape and eventual death of the Nirbhaya case in December, 
2012 jolted the entire nation about the safety, security and value of life of a woman 
leading to mass protests across the country.  Inspite of all this, the Committee fails 
to see any pro -active role of the Commission with respect to safeguarding rights of 
women.  The Committee firmly believes that bein g the national body for women's 
rights, the Commission needs to widen its scope of activities beyond its present set of 
activities.  Vigorous and concerted efforts need to be taken by the Commission , 
especially with respect to crimes against women.   
 
13.4 The Committee has been given to understand that presently the Ministry does not 
have any specific scheme to help victims of rape or molestation.  Two schemes i.e 
Swadhar and Short Stay Homes provided temporary shelter, food, clothing, vocational 
training, counseling etc to women in difficult circumstances.  Also, gender sensitization 
was taken up through different platforms.  NCW itself was engaged in sponsoring a 
number of awareness generation programmes and call for investigations into specific 
problems or situations arising out of atrocities against women.  The disturbing rise in rape 
and molestation cases in the country in general and Delhi in particular should have been 
an area of concern and focus.  The Committee would like to emphasize  that NCW 
needs to concretize it efforts in such a way so as to force change by striving to make 
laws much more stringent and also actively campaign for the safety and security of 
women force.  The focus should not only be on providing relief to the victims of rape 
and molestation but also on prohibiting the occurrence of such crimes against 
women through active policing and other women -orientated initiatives.  The 
Committee hopes that NCW would engage in active and aggressive safeguarding  of 
the interests of women.    
 
13.5 Committee's attention has been drawn to the issues pertaining to NRI marriages 
for which the National Commission for Women has been nominated as the coordinating 

Agency at the National level by the Government of India in April, 2009 based on the 
recommendation of the Parliamentary Committee on Empowerment of Women on the 
subject 'Plight of Indian Woman deserted by NRI husbands'.  The NRI Cell was formally 
inaugurated in NCW on 24 th September, 2009 to deal with complaints received from 
India and abroad resulting from cross country marriages wherein there was any 
deprivation of women's rights or any issue involving grave injustice to women.  Since its 
inception, around 1303 complaint have been registered till date i.e 30 th March, 2013 in 
the NRI Cell, out of which 190 complaints had been closed for various reasons. 
 
13.6 The Committee was given to understand that NRI Cell of NCW took 100 per cent 
complaints registered with it and took due suitable action on each and every complaint 
registered.  The complai nts which had not been closed had been taken up for suitable 
action and were considered pending for various reasons.  The complaints registered in 
NRI Cell since its inception in September, 2009 broadly comprised following 
categorization desertion, dowry-demand, capturing of passport by husband/in-Laws, child 
custody problems, apprehension of husband leaving the country, seeking legal/financial 
assistance under MOIA Scheme, issuance of duplicate passport, seeking return of 
Istridhan and maintenance, police apathy, service of judicial processes abroad and to 
know the where abouts of husband living abroad.   
 
13.7 The Committee notes that data of the total number of complaints since September, 
2009 which is as follows:- 
Year Total Number of Complaints 
 State-wise Country-wise 
September, 2009 to 
31st March, 2010 
209 251 
2010-11 271 343 
2011-12 266 328

The Committee finds that the total number of complaints with respect to NRI marriages 
state-wise and country-wise has been on an increase ov er the past few years.  State -wise 
data reveals maximum number of complaints from Delhi, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, 
Punjab etc.  Country -wise data indicates that maximum number of complaints got 
reported from India and USA. 

 
13.8 The Committee has been g iven to understand that NCW largely adopted a 
convergence approach among different Ministries and efforts were made to coordinate 
jointly on taking up matters for the victims with respective authorities.  Recent initiatives 
taken by NCW regarding problems of Indian brides deserted by NRI/Overseas husbands 
included registration and processing of complaints of deserted women by NRI/Overseas 
husbands, attempt to spread awareness on the subject and to provide information on legal 
and other remedies to innocent India woman trapped in such marriages in informative 
booklet 'Abandoned Indian Women Trapped in NRI Marriages', 'Nowhere Brides -A 
report on NRI marriages' and a brochure 'Problems relating to NRI marriages -Dos and 
Donts', pro-active steps in co -operation with State Governments of Punjab and Gujarat, 
link with list of empanelled foreign NGOs under the scheme for providing legal/financial 
assistance/rehabilitation to Indian women deserted by overseas Indian spouses etc. 
 
13.9 The Committee appreciates the initiatives taken by the NRI Cell of the NCW.  
However, inspite of these, the Committee notes the increasing number of complaints 
state-wise and country -wise.  Out of 1308 cases, only 190 had been disposed off.  A 
large number of cases still remained pending.   The Committee is of the view that all 
out efforts need to be taken for disposal of cases within a specified time.  Further, 
the Committee feels that focus of the NRI Cell should be first and foremost to 
prevent such marriages wherein the NRI groom is alr eady married or planning to 
run away.  The Committee would like to suggest that before such a marriage takes 
place, the concerned country where the NRI resides can issue an Unmarried 
Certificate before he could be permitted to get married to an Indian brid e. The 
Committee also feels that there is a need for sensitizing the parents of prospective 
brides in this regard, especially in those states where such marriages are taking 
place more frequently.  State Commission for Women can be involved in this 
exercise.  This obviously necessitated co -operation with other countries and also 
changes in the Marriage Registration Form by the Office of the Registrar General 
of Marriage.  Further, all details of the NRI groom about his residence and 
workplace etc must be br ought on record before any marriage takes place so as to 
catch hold of the groom in case of desertion of Indian brides.  This measure would 

help in curbing ill -intentioned marriages of NRI grooms and doing justice with the 
Indian brides.   
 
13.10 The Committee has been informed that a five member Expert Committee and a 
four member Sub-Committee was constituted for addressing various issues and problems 
pertaining to NRI/Overseas marriages and its report submitted but the NCW felt that the 
issue needed in depth  research and consultations with different stake holders to come out 
with a reasoned document covering identification, assessment and management of the 
problem and suggesting specific amendments to the various provision of different laws of 
the country in order to benefit the affected women.  The final report, of the Committee is, 
however, awaited.  The Committee is relieved to know that a Committee and Sub -
Committee has been formed by NCW specifically to look into the problems of 
NRI/Overseas marriages .  The Committee hopes that the final report would 
definitely come out with stringent measures including sound and verified 
documentation of the NRI grooms so that the problems arising generally in such 
marriages are curtailed to a great extent.  The Commi ttee believes that in the 
interest of women going for overseas marriage, the NCW should expedite the report 
of its Committee and Sub -Committee so as to prevent other women from being 
duped or harassed by NRI grooms.  The Committee would like to emphasize t hat 
NCW needs to play pro -active role for disposal of pending cases/complaints and 
devise a mechanism for preventing overseas marriages which are ill- intentioned. 
 
XIV. NATIONAL NUTRITION MISSION (NNM) 
 
14.1 A National Nutrition Mission (NNM) was set up u nder the Chairmanship of the 
Prime Minister in 2003.  Subsequently in 2008, the Prime Minister's National Council on 
India's Nutritional challenges was constituted.  The Council decided to (i) strengthen and 
restructure the ICDS Scheme (ii) introduce a mul ti-sectoral programme to address 
maternal and child malnutrition in selected 200 high burden districts (iii) introducing a 
nationwide information, education and communication (IEC) campaign against 
malnutrition and (iv) making nutrition a focus in the prog rammes and schemes of line 
Ministries.  
 

14.2 Allocation for National Nutrition Mission and utilization therefor reveals a very 
interesting picture as shown below:- 
                     (` in crore) 
Year BE RE Expenditure 
2010-11 1.00 1.00 0.00 
2011-12 100.00 100.00 0.00 
2012-13 250.00 83.00 52.55  
 
In the years 2010 -11 and 2011-12, funds remained totally un -utilized because of non -receipt 
of final approval from the Planning Commission.  In 2012 -13 `250.00 crore had been 
allocated to the Scheme which wa s reduced to `83.00 crore at the RE stage , thereby 
witnessing a substantial reduction.  The Committee has been given to understand by the 
Ministry that allocation of `250.00 crore was made for two components of the Mission i.e an 
IEC compaign for malnutrit ion for which `50.00 crore was kept as a token provision at BE 
stage.  However, the launch of the IEC campaign by Hon'ble President of India was done on 
the 19th  November and it was rolled out on the 28 th December, 2012.  Given the lag -time of 
coordination among agencies and payment of bills etc from DAVP and other I & B agency, 
the provision for `70-73 crore was considered adequate at the RE stage.  For the multi -
sectoral Nutrition Action Programme, after discussion with the Planning Commission and 
PMO an d given the limited resources , allocation indicated to the Ministry, the scope and 
approach of the programme was revised in December, 2012/January, 2013.  Comments had 
been received and the final EFC was under submission.  A token provision of about `10.00 
crore had been kept for this purpose at the RE stage. 
 
14.3 The Committee notes that the Mission had taken off last y ear only i.e 2012 -13 
with under -utilization of funds.  The years 2010 -11 and 2011 -12 had nil utilization of 
funds and the Scheme could not  take off due to the pending final approval of the 
Planning Commission.  The Committee is of the view that Nutrition Mission was of 
immense importance given the nutritional status of the women and children in the 
country.  With the launch of the IEC Campai gn, the Mission had taken off but only 
after inordinate delay.  The Committee would like to emphasize on the other component 
of a framework of multi -sectoral programme to address the maternal and children 

nutrition, in selected 200 high -burden districts which had been prepared and proposed 
to bring together with various national programmes through strong institutional and 
pragmatic convergence at the State, District, Block and Village levels.  Since the multi -
sectoral Nutrition Programme had been revised, i t was likely to be delayed further in 
view of necessary approvals.   The Committee hopes that all initial procedural and 
administrative steps are cleared without any further delay for the implementation of 
both the components of the scheme.  
 
14.4 Nutrition was essential for human development but a situational analysis of maternal 
and child under nutrition levels remained persistently and unacceptably high.  It was a 
complex and multi -dimensional issue affected by poverty, inadequage food consumption, 
inequitable food distribution, improper infant and child feeding and care practices, equity and 
gender imbalances, poor sanitary and environmental conditions and restricted access to 
quality health, education and social care services.  The following table highl ighted certain 
facts about nutrition challenges in India as given in the Report of the Working Group on 
Nutrition in Twelfth Plan:-

nutrition status of the most vulnerable age group of children was a sensitive proxy

effectiveness and efficiency of social development investments.  This was through 
inclusion of the most vulnerable and those most at risk through synergy of multi -sectoral 
action by catalyzing reforms in health and child care and through strengthening of 
participatory processes and capacities for assessment, analysis and informed action that 
also improved governance processes and mechanisms.

14.6 The Committee is constrained to note that no data is a vailable regarding the 
achievement of many of monitorable targets set for the Eleventh Plan period like the 
reduction of  malnutrition among children of age group 0 -3 year to half of 46 per 
cent, reducing anaemia among women and girls by 50 per cent by the  end of 2012 
etc.  Even the status of other targets reveal under -achievement in many respects.  
The Committee feels that the performance in the Eleventh Plan period to tackle 
under-nutrition, mal-nutrition and related aspects ha s not been seriously address ed 
by the Ministry.  Concerted and aggressive efforts for co -ordinating and 
administrating various measures of several Ministries/Departments to tackle under -
nutrition and mal -nutrition need to be taken by the Ministry to implement various 
nutritional intervention measures, direct or indirect.  Focused attention needs to be 
given to the formation of State Nutrition Councils in high burden States. 
 
14.7 The Committee has been given to understand that the vision for the Twelfth Plan 
on nutrition was to ensure  'Nutrition Security for all', especially the more vulnerable 
infants and young children, adolescent girls and women, across the life cycle fulfilling 

their rights to nutrition, health and human development to their full potential.  The focus 
was to be on the following monitorable targets during the plan period:- 
 Reduction by 25 percentage points in underweight amongst children under three 
years and under five years; 
 Reduction in the prevalence of moderate and severe anaemia in children and 
pregnant women and adolescents by 50 per cent of the current level; 
 Improvement in early initiation of breastfeeding by 50 per cent of the current 
level; 
 Improvement in exclusive breastfeeding till six months by 50 per cent of the 
current level; 
 Improvement in introductio n of complementary feeding after six months by 50 
per cent of the current level; and  
 100 per cent consumption of adequately iodated salt (15 PPM) at the house hold 
level. 
 
In order to achieve the above -mentioned targets, the key priorities in the Twelfth Plan 
period were to be on implementation of the decisions of the PM's National Council on 
addressing India's nutrition challenges.  It also envisaged putting in place institutional 
arrangements, implementation and monitoring of multi -sectoral State/Distric t Nutrition 
Plan of Action led by State/District Nutrition Councils especially in high burden districts 
and universalization of core multi -sectoral interventions for addressing nutrition 
challenges etc. 
 
14.8 The Committee takes into cognizance the multi -faceted nutrition challenges 
the country is facing .  Even though the achievement of monitorable targets of the 
Eleventh Plan period has not been very encouraging, the Committee hopes that the 
monitorable targets set for the Twelfth Plan period are achieved through sustained 
and concerted efforts of the Ministry with the co -operation of all the States/UTs for 
setting up the necessary structures for effec tive implementation of multi -sectoral 
interventions for addressing nutrition challenges and continuous monitoring and 
surveillance of the nutrition status across the country. 
 
XV. INFORMATION, MASS MEDIA AND PUBLICATION 
 
15.1 Awareness about women and children -related issues and variety of schemes 
initiated for their welfare and protection , both in the general public as well as 
implementing agencies is the most crucial requirement so as to sensitize all concerned.  

The Committee observes that substantive funds are being duly allocated  for this purpose  
every year.  On perusal of the trend of allocation of funds a nd utilization thereof,  the 
Committee notes that during the Eleventh Plan, against an allocation of  `213.00 crore, 
utilization reported at the end of the Plan period is only `135.39 crore.  During the first 
year of the Twelfth Plan period also, only `1.96 crore could be spent by the 31 st 
December, 2012, although provision of `50.00 crore was there. 
 
15.2 The Committee strongly feels that a comprehensive advocacy and awareness 
generation policy and plan of action has to be developed and implemented that wil l 
ensure awareness generation and public education of existing policies and 
programmes for women  and children at all levels.  In addition, a national 
awareness campaign having involvement of all concerned has to be launched.  Only 
then, public at large an d other stakeholders can be sensitized in the real sense.  The 
Committee is of the view that all efforts made in bringing out such a large number 
of laws and allied schemes/programmes can register their impact only if awareness 
about them is there both in the designated authorities and implementing agencies 
and also targeted beneficiaries. 
 
XVI. GENDER BUDGETING 
 
16.1 Gender Budgeting is a powerful tool for addressing gender -based  disparities and 
achieving women empowerment through mainstreaming gender concern across sectors.  
The Ministry, the nodal Ministry for gender budgeting, has been pursuing with Central 
level Ministries/Departments and State Governments for adoption of gender budgeting 
for enhancing gender responsiveness of all programmes and schemes. 
 
16.2 The Committee notes that so far 56 Ministries/Departments  have set up Gender 
Budgeting Cells.  States like Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Bihar, 
Uttarakhand, Kerala, Odisha, Himachal Pradesh, Rajasthan and Jammu & Kashmir have 
undertaken var ious Gender Budgeting initiatives.  The Ministry proposes to take up 
Gender Audit of a few critical schemes with focus on the analysis of the 

programme/scheme guidelines, actual allocations, beneficiary incidence/impact analysis 
and the delivery mechanisms. 
 
16.3 The Committee finds that considerable progress has been made in this new 
area of fund management across the Ministries both at the Central and State level 
from the perspective of women specific concerns.  However, further steps have to be 
taken to further institutionalize the Gender Budget ing proceses.  The focus now 
should be to strengthen and empower the General Budgeting Cells to enable them to 
undertake the envisaged role.  It would be more result -oriented if 
Ministries/Departments are encourage d to undertake gender audits of major 
programmes, schemes and policies. 
 
16.4 Like Gender Budgeting, Child Budgeting can be considered another major 
initiative in sensitizing and institutionalizing child -related concerns.  For this 
purpose, the Committee n otes that the Ministry will have to build capacities to 
analyse the Central and State budgets and their impact on the outcomes for 
children. 
 
XVII. LEGISLATIONS RELATING TO WOMEN AND CHILDREN 
 
17.1 Over the years, a number of legislations have been enacted  both for women and 
children.  Inspite of our society having undergone a lot of changes, the status of women 
and children still remains quite vulnerable.  The process of enacting new laws keeping 
pace with the need for giving a better and well -protected en vironment to women and 
children continues.  The Committee observes that quite a few new laws are in the pipeline 
and there is a need also for having some more such laws.  While appreciating these 
developments, the Committee also strongly feels that time ha s come for reviewing the 
existing laws with a view to bring out changes wherever required.  The Committee finds 
that exercise in this regard has already been initiated by the Ministry in consultations with 
various stakeholders. 
 
17.2 A draft Amendment Bill  on the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 was prepared in 
consultation with the Ministry of Law and Justice, based on few amendments suggested 
by the National Commission for Women.  However, in view of a number of 
representations received against the proposed am endments, a series of consultations were 

held with State Governments and other stakeholders.  The Cabinet Note on amendments 
to the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 is presently under finalization in the Ministry.  The 
growing incidence of trafficking for prost itution is a matter of growing concern.  Certain 
amendments are proposed to the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956 which includes 
deletion of those sections that revictimize the victims and more stringent punishment for 
perpetrators.  The National Comm ission for Women has taken up the review of the Medical 
Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971 with a view to examine whether the provisions of the 
Act require any amendment. 
 
17.3 Committee's attention has been drawn by a number of very pertinent 
suggestions/recommendations made by the Working Group on Women's Agency and 
Empowerment for Twelfth Plan.  While suggesting  changes in some provisions of the 
Dowry Prohibition act, 1961, the Working Group has also recommended improving the 
implementation of the Act by appointing sufficient number of dedicated and full time Dowry 
Prohibition officers and also undertaking training and capacity -building of law enforcement 
agencies and the judiciary.  The Working Group has also advocated extensive amendments in 
the Preven tion of Immoral Trafficking Act.  Emphasizing the need for increasing control 
about trafficking menace, the Working Group has pointed out the need for undertaking a 
mapping of areas vulnerable to trafficking, along with having designated courts and fast 
tracking the judicial process.  Similarly, the Working Group has opined that a multi -pronged 
approach was required to implement the PCPNDT Act, to amend it wherever necessary, 
create awareness about the Act and to gender sensitize the persons in-charge of implementing 
the various provisions of the Act. Committee's attention has also been drawn to the 
recommendation for having a comprehensive stand-alone law to deal with killings and crimes 
in the name of honour and also a comprehensive Right to Marital Proper ty Act applicable to 
all communities. The specific suggestions made by the Working Group in this regard merit 
urgent attention of all concerned.   
 
17.4 The Committee also takes note of the recommendations of the Working Group on 
Child Rights for bringing out modifications in the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) 
Act, National Commission for Protection of Child Rights Act and also having a review of the 
impact of the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006. 
 
17.5 The Committee observes that the task  before the Ministry so far as review of 
existing laws relating to women and children and also enacting some new laws is 

concerned is quite an elaborate exercise.  The Committee would appreciate that this 
exercise is carried forward and completed in a miss ion mode.  At the same time, the 
Committee would like to emphasize that there are quite a few laws which  inspite of 
being enacted some years ago have virtually remained un -implemented as the proposed 
law-enforcing authorities in States are simply not in pl ace.  One such example is the 
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 as only six State Governments 
have appointed independent Protection officers so far.  A Scheme for assistance to 
States for implementation of this Act has been drafted only recently and yet to be 
activated.  Similarly, State Commissions for the Protection of Child Rights are yet to be 
set up by many State Governments.   
 
17.6 The Committee would also take the opportunity to impress upon the Ministry 
not to allow recently enac ted laws like the Protection of Children from Sexual Offence 
Act and Protection of Women from Sexual Offences at Workplace Act remaining 
unimplemented for want of implementing authorities at various levels. 
 
XVIII. CONCLUSION 
 
18.1 The Ministry of Women an d Child Development is the nodal Ministry having 
the mandate to take care of all areas of women and children related concerns.  To be the 
designated authority of that segment of the population of the country which translates 
into more than 70 per cent of t he total population and that too the most vulnerable is 
indeed a very heavy responsibility for a Ministry.  The Committee is well aware that the 
Ministry has been carrying forward its multi -faceted mandate inspite of having very 
apparent and unavoidable li mitations.  The Committee also knows that all the schemes 
and policies formulated by the Ministry and various laws enacted so far are to be 
implemented by various State Governments, that too across the country.  Nobody can 
doubt the well -intention behind a ll the policy measures which inspite of being well -
conceptualized generally have to face practical problems at ground levels, sometimes 
due to very genuine State –specific limitations.  Another area of concern for the 
Committee is very low level of awarenes s about women and children related schemes, 
non-availability of institutional mechanisms at various levels.  The Committee strongly 
feels that a sustained effort at all India level has to be built up for increasing the 
awareness level.  Awareness has also to be built up for bringing about a change in the 

thinking and mind set of our public so as to adequately sensitize them about women and 
children related concerns.

REPORT
I. INTRODUCTION
1.1 The Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports is entrusted with the responsibilities relating to the
development of Youth and Adolescents, and the functions of the Central Government with regard
to Sports and Physical Education. There are two separate Departments viz. Department of Youth
Affairs and Department of Sports.
1.2 The subject “Youth Affairs” is dealt in the Department of Youth Affairs of the Ministry. As
per the initial figures of the 2011 Census, the current youth population in the country including
adolescents is around 550 million. It is indeed vital to utilize this “demographic dividend” and
channelize the youth and their creative energies for nation-building. The Department of Youth
Affairs is implementing a large number of schemes for youth and adolescents development which
focus on three key thrust areas viz., Personality Development, Preparation for Work Participation/
Employability and Empowerment. The programmes of the Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan (NYKS)
focus towards rural youth and vast network of youth clubs and volunteers who undertake number
of activities for youth at the grassroot level. National Service Scheme (NSS) provides a platform
for students to enhance their personality through community service.
1.3 The Secretary, Youth Affairs in her presentation before the Committee on the 25
th March,
2013 gave an overview of status of plan allocation and utilization thereof during 2012-13. She
informed that during the year, the Department, through its available resources and tapping of funds
from other Departments, trained youth under various skill development training programmes across
the country. At present, about 50 lakh rural youths were associated with Nehru Yuva Kendra
Sangathan and 32 lakh with National Service Scheme. The Committee was given an idea about the
initiatives taken by the Department to start the process of skill development so as to scale up these
activities during the Twelfth Plan. The Department had been in consultation with the Office of
Advisor to Prime Minister on Skill Development on ‘Repositioning NSS’ by introducing ‘Skill
Training’ so that the graduating youth could acquire job-related skills through immersive community
projects.
1.4 The Secretary drew the attention of the Committee to non-availability of required Plan funds
inspite of there being a huge demand for additional hours and additional colleges to be sanctioned
under NSS. Target of enrolling 55 million volunteers under NSS during the Eleventh Plan period
also remained un-achieved. To fill this gap, self-financing units were being started in institutions
which would work as per the existing guidelines of NSS. This initiative had led to setting up of
1100 self-financing units across the country with approximately one lakh volunteers.
1.5 The Committee was also given an idea about the initiatives taken by the Department under
the other Flagship Programme of NYKS. Training programmes with various agencies like Tata
Consultancy Services, Ministries of Home Affairs, Social Justice and Empowerment, Health &
Family Welfare, Women and Child Development, Rural Development and Universities were being
undertaken. However, this Scheme was also not giving the targeted results due to shortage of
funds. The Secretary also touched upon other schemes being implemented by the Department.
1.6 The Department of Sports in the Ministry deals with “Sports”. With reference to
competitive sports and promotion of excellence at the national and international levels, the
responsibility for development of different disciplines rests primarily with the National Sports
Federations (NSFs) concerned, which are registered autonomous organizations. The Government of
India has been supplementing the efforts of the State Governments through certain schemes of

2
financial assistance for sports infrastructure. The Central Government directly, and also through the
Sports Authority of India (SAI), provides financial assistance and a variety of facilities, for
competition exposure, training/coaching etc., to NSFs for preparation of teams for international
events. SAI also has a number of schemes for the spotting and nurturing of young talent. In
addition, the Department is also implementing schemes for providing incentives to sportspersons to
encourage them to take up sports as a career. It is also concerned with physical education, an
aspect of physical fitness as a vital ingredient of youth development, as well as means of enhancing
the sporting abilities of the young.
1.7 The Secretary, Department of Sports also appeared before the Committee on the 25
th March,
2013 and gave an overview of the functioning of the Department during 2012-13 and also the
vision for nurturing sports talent in the country. The Committee was given to understand that the
Department could achieve the optimum utilisation level of allocated funds during 2012-13 with
expenditure being duly accounted for. Inspite of there being massive cut in the fund allocation
during the last quarter of 2012-13, it was ensured that the programmes did not suffer. Another
highlight was improvement in the functioning of National Sports Federations across the country.
The Federations were now working to develop a long term plan for their individual sports with
Olympics, 2020 as the target.
1.8 The Secretary also informed the Committee that the Panchayat Yuva Krida Khel
Abhiyan(PYKKA) was being re-structured in coordination with other schemes like NREGA. The
other major initiative was setting up of the Institute of Sports Medicine and the Institute of Sports
Coaching. Feasibility Report on the two proposed Institutes being done by the National Skill
Development Corporation was expected by June and the work on the two Institutes may start by
November-December in this year.
1.9 The Secretary then dwelt upon the biggest initiative, Scheme of Identification and Nurturing
of Sports Talent which would be a ten-year project. Through the competitions held under PYKKA,
100 talented children in the age group of 6-10 years would be selected from every district of the
country. These children would be admitted in 700 District Sports Schools. The talented children
would ultimately get the opportunity to be trained in SAI Centres of Excellence.

III. NEHRU YUVA KENDRA SANGATHAN (NYKS)
3.1 Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan (NYKS) is an autonomous body of the Ministry of Youth
Affairs and Sports. NYKS has its presence in 623 districts of the country. It has become one of
the largest Youth Organisations in the world, reaching out to village-based youth clubs. These Youth
Clubs work in the areas like education and training, awareness generation, skill development and
self-employment, entrepreneurial development, thrift and co-operation, besides development of the
body through sports and adventure and mind through sustained exposure to new ideas and
development strategies. For implementation of the programmes, every district Nehru Yuva Kendra
(NYK) has a trained cadre of District Youth Coordinator, National Youth Corps (NYC) V olunteers
and Youth leaders.
3.2 NYKS accomplishes its task through two categories of programmes i.e.  Regular
Programmes and Schemes assigned to it by the Ministry and Special Programmes undertaken in
collaboration with other Ministries and organisations. During 2012-13, NYKS undertook various
important programmes. 12,307 office bearers of Mentor Youth Clubs were trained. 1000 Members
of Youth Clubs of participating 100 district NYKS visited important places including historical sites,
tourist spots, academic, scientific and technological establishments of host 100 district NYKs. In
606 districts, 3030 skill upgradation training programmes were organised in which 58,882 women

5
participated. SMART courses were run in 66 selected districts. Besides that, 3698 National Youth
Corps volunteers were given Refresher Training and Skill Development Training was provided to
2947 outgoing volunteers in the Agricultural and Allied field through KVK. Awareness and Education
for the Prevention of Drug Abuse and Alcoholism was implemented in Punjab and Manipur which
covered 3000 villages in 75 Blocks of 10 Districts of Punjab and 750 villages of 25 Blocks in
7 Districts of Manipur. Under the Programme of Capacity Building of NYKS Youth Clubs for Social
Empowerment of workers under MGNREGA, workers in 80,000 villages were empowered with
latest updates on the MGNREGA Act. Lastly, NYKS in collaboration with UN Fund for Population
Activities implemented a Project on ‘Adolescent Health and Development in 10 districts of Bihar,
MP, Maharashtra, Odisha and Rajasthan.
3.3 The Secretary during her presentation before the Committee informed that under the NYKS
they have taken up initiatives for the skill development programme through the Tata Consultancy
Services(TCS). They have taken up the training programmes, through the TCS, in four States –
Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka. About 2000 people will be trained over a period
of three to six months and they will also be provided placements. Similarly, in a pilot project they
are taking up training programme of about 2000 boys and girls from the naxal affected districts
of Bastar in Chattisgarh through the Ministry of Home Affairs. They are also trying to take up such
programmes with other Ministries. There is a `2.20 crore proposed project with the Ministry of
Road Transport for using services of volunteers on the National Highways for providing first-aid
and emergency medical facilities to road accident victims on pilot basis. There is also a project on
Prevention of Drug Abuse and Alcoholism in Punjab with the Ministry of Social Justice and
Empowerment. The project has been started in two districts and will cover other districts as well
for which an additional allocation of `6.70 crore may be given. There are other schemes such as
empowering of rural women through social mobilization and community participation by
convergence of schemes at the village level with the Ministry of Women and Child Development.
Then, there is a proposal for deploying youth professionals with NYKS across the country under
CAPART with the Ministry of Rural Development.
3.4 The Committee is encouraged to find that the Department has come up with various
projects with different agencies, private as well as Government for skill development and
training programmes. However, it appears that these projects/schemes are only in their
initial stages and as mentioned by the Secretary are being constrained by the fund crunch.
Before initiating these projects, the Department should formulate a policy framework or a
road map on the convergence of the scheme with other agencies or Ministries in the matter
of allocation of funds and proper utilization of the volunteers.
3.5 On a specific query whether all the Nehru Yuva Kendras have the required work force, the
Department informed the Committee that as per the sanctioned strength, each Kendra of NYKS was
to be manned by one District Youth Coordinator (DYC), one Accountant-Clerk-Typist(ACT) and one
Multi Tasking Staff(MTS). At present, there was a shortage of 327 DYCs and 199 ACTs. 12,000
volunteers had been allotted to NYKS under the Scheme of National Youth Corps (NYC). These
volunteers were involved in the implementation of different programmes/activities of NYKS. The
volunteers were deployed in all the 623 districts of NYKS @ 2 volunteers per block. As on date,
9300 volunteers were in position and the selection of remaining volunteers against the allocation was
in process. Abut 12,000 volunteers would be in position by the first week of April, 2013.

• To review the structure of the organization along with the feeder cadre, keeping in view
the findings of (i) above;

3.8 The Committee is constrained to observe that the entire exercise will be a long
drawn affair and will perhaps continue during the entire Twelfth Plan period. That will also

3.9 The Committee was informed that against the allocation of `134.84 crore in RE 2012-13
(Plan `106.38 crore and Non-Plan `28.46 crore), the anticipated expenditure was `134.84 crore
For 2013-14, against a projected requirement of `370.30 crore (Plan `336.30 crore and Non-Plan

3.10 The Committee observes that continuing with its track-record of previous years, there has
been optimum utilisation of allocated funds by NYKS during 2012-13. Nobody can dispute the fact
that NYKS is not only one of the major youth organisations under the Ministry, particularly with
reference to the rural areas but also a major purveyor of schemes and programmes, in terms of
designing and implementing them. The Committee also takes note of the approach of the Twelfth
Plan – review of the existing sectoral programmes and schemes and bringing into them the required
specific focus and re-orientation and their expansion to cover the whole country and diverse groups
and ultimately empower and enable the youth to become effective and productive participants in
the social, economic and political development of the country.
3.11 The Committee views with serious concern that the projected requirement of
`2182.35 crore for NYKS for the Twelfth Plan remains totally ignored, inspite of optimum
utilisation of allocated funds during the Eleventh Plan period as well as the first year of the
Twelfth Plan. Factors like introduction of some new schemes/programmes, projected
enhancement of the Regular Programme coverage from 501 Districts to 623 Districts, filling
up of vacant posts of NYKS functionaries and payment of enhanced salary to them have to
be addressed in the right earnest. The Committee, accordingly, strongly recommends
enhanced allocation for NYKS for 2013-14. Need of the hour is to utilise the demographic
dividend accruing due to the phenomenal rise in the youth population of the country and
channelize the youth and their creative energies for nation-building. For achieving this
objective, core requirement of funds has to be taken care of.
3.12 The Committee observes that there are some major proposals which have to be
implemented during the Twelfth Plan period as indicated below:
– Establishment of Regional Youth Centres, Yuva Utthan evam Vikas Kendras at
Bangalore, Gandhinagar, Bhubaneswar, Chandigarh and Guwahati
– Information Technology
– Construction of NYKS Office Buildings

3.13 Committee’s attention has been drawn by the long pending project of construction of
National Youth Centre building in Alipur, New Delhi. The Committee is surprised to note

complex at Alipur could be taken by the Board of Governors on the 27
th July, 1994.
Thereafter, it took another 16 years for the Board of Governors, i.e. on the 2 nd February,
2010 to taka a decision to prepare a Concept Paper/Master Plan for the development of

the non-plan allocation in both 2012-13 and 2013-14. That clearly shows that the project is

3.14 It would be 30 years by the end of 2013-14 when the required land was allotted for
National Youth Centre. Normally, non-availability of land is cited as the primary reason for
implementation of a project. Here, the story is entirely different. Piece of land is duly

operate from rented premises. If the project had been taken in the right earnest in 1984

requirement. The Committee has no doubt in saying that the estimate of `516.17 crore
projected in 2010 would fall behind if the project starts during 2013-14.  The Committee

the same completed during the Twelfth Plan period only.
3.15 The Committee has been closely monitoring the proposal for inclusion of 122 uncovered

functionaries. Even the functional Kendras are not well equipped with the required
